content: The proton is a subatomic particle characterized by a positive electric charge of one fundamental unit, specifically 1.60217653(14)×10^−19 coulombs. Its diameter is approximately 1.65×10^-15 meters, and its mass is 938.27231 MeV/c², equivalent to 1.00727646688(13) atomic mass units or 1.6726×10^-27 kilograms. This makes the proton about 1836 times more massive than an electron. Historical Discovery of the Proton The discovery of the proton is primarily attributed to Ernest Rutherford in 1918. Rutherford observed that when alpha particles were directed into nitrogen gas, scintillation detectors detected the presence of hydrogen nuclei. He concluded that the hydrogen nuclei must have originated from the nitrogen atoms, suggesting that nitrogen contains hydrogen nuclei. Rutherford proposed that the hydrogen nucleus, known to have an atomic number of 1, was a fundamental particle. Before Rutherford's work, Eugene Goldstein had observed canal rays, which were streams of positively charged ions moving in the opposite direction of electrons in cathode ray tubes. Goldstein hypothesized the existence of a positively charged particle to balance the atom's overall neutrality. However, his experiments revealed that the charge-to-mass ratio of these particles varied depending on the gas used in the tube. This variability indicated that the particles he observed were ions, not protons. Goldstein abandoned his work on this topic, though he expressed an intention to revisit it, but his contributions were largely overlooked. Structural and Physical Properties of Protons Protons are classified as spin-½ fermions and belong to the baryon family. They are composed of three quarks: two up quarks and one down quark. These quarks are held together by the strong nuclear force, which is mediated by gluons. Protons, along with neutrons, are nucleons and can be bound together by the nuclear force to form atomic nuclei. The simplest atomic nucleus, that of the most common hydrogen isotope, consists of a single proton without any neutrons. In contrast, the nuclei of heavier hydrogen isotopes, such as deuterium and tritium, contain one or more neutrons. The number of protons in an atom's nucleus determines its chemical properties and defines the element. The combined number of protons and neutrons in a nucleus determines the specific isotope of that element. The Antiproton The antiproton, the antiparticle of the proton, was discovered in 1955 by Emilio Segrè and Owen Chamberlain, an achievement that earned them the 1959 Nobel Prize in Physics. According to CPT symmetry, the properties of particles and their corresponding antiparticles are tightly constrained. For instance, the charges of the proton and antiproton must sum to zero, a relationship that has been experimentally verified to a precision of one part in 10^8. Similarly, the masses of the proton and antiproton have been shown to be equal to better than one part in 10^8. By confining antiprotons in a Penning trap, the charge-to-mass ratio of the proton and antiproton has been tested to a precision of 1 part in 9×10^11. Protons in High-Energy Physics Protons are particularly useful in high-energy physics experiments due to their stability and relatively large mass compared to electrons. They are commonly used in particle colliders, such as the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN and the Tevatron at Fermilab. Protons also constitute the majority of cosmic rays that interact with Earth's atmosphere. However, studying high-energy proton collisions is more complex than studying electron collisions because protons are composite particles made up of quarks and gluons. Understanding the internal structure of protons requires the application of quantum chromodynamics, the theory describing the strong nuclear force.
